title: Dodgers' Ohtani Confirms He Won’t Be Fully Healthy for Playoffs, ESPN Reports
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers ace Shohei Ohtana entered the National League Division Series acknowledging that lingering discomfort in his left knee and right biceps will force him to “manage” his body rather than expect full health. The two‑way phenom, who has been a dominant force on both the mound and at the plate all season, said the recent stretch of games has been “very productive,” but he remains realistic about the physical toll the marathon campaign has taken.

Ohtani’s injuries began to surface in mid‑summer when a subtle wobble in his left knee and a nagging biceps strain started to limit his explosiveness. While the Dodgers’ medical staff kept him on the roster, the star’s performance metrics dipped slightly, prompting speculation about his long‑term durability. Over the past two weeks, however, Ohtani has logged a string of solid outings, posting a .312 batting average with three home runs and a 2.71 ERA in his starts. “My swing feels better, my feel is better,” he told reporters after a 4‑2 win that clinched the division title, underscoring the progress he has made despite the aches.

The Dodgers, now facing the Atlanta Braves in the NLDS, must weigh Ohtani’s limited availability against the high stakes of postseason baseball. Manager Dave Roberts has already hinted at a flexible rotation plan, potentially shortening Ohtani’s innings on the mound while maximizing his impact at the plate. “We’ll keep him in the lineup as much as we can, but we’re also going to protect him,” Roberts said, noting that the team’s depth in the bullpen and the emergence of young hitters like Gavin Lux give them leeway to adjust. The strategic calculus mirrors the Dodgers’ approach in previous postseason runs, where star players were occasionally rested or used in a reduced role to preserve health for the championship stretch.

Analysts are divided on how much Ohtani’s condition could affect the series outcome. Some argue that even a slightly compromised pitcher can dominate when he’s on the mound, given his elite velocity and command. Others point to the physical demands of a full nine‑inning start, especially with a compromised knee that could hinder his delivery and fielding. On the offensive side, Ohtani’s bat remains a potent weapon; his ability to drive the ball deep and work the count could offset any reduction in his pitching workload. “If he can stay in the lineup for at least five at‑bats each game, the Dodgers still have a huge advantage,” said former MLB analyst Jeff Passan.

The broader context of Ohtani’s situation highlights the evolving nature of two‑way players in modern baseball. Since his historic debut with the Los Angeles Angels, Ohtani has redefined expectations, showing that a player can excel simultaneously as a starter and a middle‑of‑order hitter. However, the physical strain of such a dual role inevitably accumulates, especially in a season that stretches into a demanding postseason. The Dodgers’ front office appears aware of this, having invested in advanced sports‑medicine resources and load‑management protocols to extend Ohtani’s effectiveness through October.

Looking ahead, the Dodgers will need to balance aggression with prudence. If Ohtani can keep his swing sharp and his arm healthy enough to pitch deep enough to give the bullpen a breather, Los Angeles retains a decisive edge in the series. Conversely, any flare‑up could force the team to lean more heavily on its supporting cast, testing the depth that has carried them through a grueling regular season. As the NLDS tip‑off looms, Ohtani’s candid admission underscores a universal postseason truth: success often hinges on how well teams adapt to the inevitable imperfections of their stars. The Dodgers’ ability to manage those imperfections will likely shape the trajectory of their championship quest.
